item.title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.27130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo

item.title: Topology optimization of shipboard components for Navy shock certification via the Dynamic Design Analysis Method
item.description: arXiv:2610.27378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shipboard equipment must survive the transient loads of underwater explosions. The U.S. Navy certifies such equipment with the Dynamic Design Analysis Method (DDAM), a modal response analysis driven by Navy shock design spectra. DDAM is well established as a verification tool, yet it is rarely used as a design driver in topology optimization. The design spectrum depends on the modal mass, a non-smooth coupling that classical sensitivity formulations do not address. This paper presents a complete differentiable formulation of the DDAM criterion for gradient-based topology optimization. Eigenvalue sensitivities follow the Fox-Kapoor method, and eigenvector sensitivities follow Nelson's method. The chain rule covers a spectral displacement that depends on both the natural frequency and the modal participation factor. Automatic differentiation assembles the sensitivity, and the engineer can certify components inside the optimization loop rather than after design. Three certification problems on a representative shipboard equipment frame demonstrate the workflow. In each, the optimizer removes 43.2% to 46.1% of the design-domain material and holds the certifying NRL Sum within 0.41% of the Navy allowable. Two companion studies follow. A compliance-optimized frame of nearly the same mass has a 5.2 Hz fundamental, outside the range the certification can qualify. Its nominal response also exceeds the allowable by a factor of 2.75. A lower bound on the mean of the two lowest eigenvalues separates the repeated pair that the demonstrations drive onto the frequency floor. The response then stops oscillating across the acceptance boundary. It ends at most 0.5% above the allowable, at a cost of under two percentage points of volume fraction.
item.dc:creator: Miguel A. Aguilo

item.title: Observability-Aligned Diffusion and Null-Space Completion for EEG Source Localization
item.description: arXiv:2610.27461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrophysiological source imaging is severely underdetermined because the lead-field matrix has limited rank relative to the source dimension and strongly correlated columns. Scalp EEG measurements constrain only the observable row-space component, leaving a high-dimensional null space unobservable. We propose a two-stage framework coupling posterior diffusion refinement with deterministic null-space completion. A minimum-norm-initialized, singular-coordinate Posterior-DDIM sampler combines a spatiotemporal diffusion prior with direction-dependent measurement reliability to refine the observable component. A frozen ridge predictor and nonlinear temporal residual network then estimate the null component under explicit projection constraints, preserving the refined row estimate and its predicted EEG exactly. All learned components are trained exclusively on simulated cortical activity and its row-null decomposition, without paired EEG-source training data. Across simulations with varying noise levels, the method achieved higher frame-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and average precision, together with lower localization error, than conventional and learning-based baselines. Exploratory evaluations on evoked EEG and simultaneous scalp EEG-stereo-EEG recordings showed condition- and event-dependent concordance with cross-modal and intracranial references.
item.dc:creator: Zirui Wen, Shihao Yang, Feng Liu

item.title: Restraint-Induced Loss in Software-Intensive Enterprises: Large A Verified Technical Economic Impact Model of Operational Downtime and Delayed Commercialization, with Tail-Risk Security Sizing and Three Enterprise Case Studies
item.description: arXiv:2610.27560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an enterprise must stop using a software component (for example, because of an interim court restraint in a technology patent dispute), the economic loss passes through a chain of technical mechanisms. Withdrawing the component exposes dependent capabilities. Fallback paths degrade throughput, correctness or feature coverage. Incident rates and recovery backlogs rise. Customers respond. Remediation programmes compete against the restraint clock, and planned launches are pushed back. This paper develops and verifies a \emph{technical--economic impact model} (TEIM) that quantifies this chain end to end as a probability distribution of present-value loss rather than as a point estimate. The technical layer combines (i)~a lattice-valued, fixed-point semantics of service dependencies with degraded fallbacks, (ii)~continuous-time Markov reliability models evaluated by uniformization and specified in continuous stochastic logic, and (iii)~a fluid queueing model of post-outage backlog. These feed (iv)~convex acute-outage loss functions with regulatory and contractual thresholds, (v)~compound-Poisson excess-incident processes, (vi)~survival-weighted functional, attrition and funding channels that provably avoid double counting, (vii)~a real-options valuation of forcibly delayed launches with an explicit closed form, and (viii)~a COCOMO~II--driven stochastic activity network for design-around and substitution strategies. We prove seven theorems and eight propositions.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Eslamimehr

item.title: TexFlow: learning crystallographic texture on SO(3) manifold via normalizing flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.28363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crystallographic texture is an important microstructural feature that statistically describes the orientations of grains in polycrystalline materials. Conventional texture analysis relies on the orientation distribution functions and pole figures, which are essential for interpreting the texture of a given material specimen but do not, by themselves, provide a direct framework for predictive modeling of process-structure-property linkages. Data- and machine learning-based approaches offer a means to address this gap; however, a key challenge lies in developing representations and learning frameworks that account for the manifold structure of rotations. In particular, many existing machine learning techniques are designed for Euclidean data and therefore are not readily applicable to rotations in the non-Euclidean group $\text{SO}(3)$. Here we introduce TexFlow, a conditional normalizing flow framework for texture modeling that learns a probability distribution over rotations in $\text{SO}(3)$ by construction. Rotations are encoded in a six-dimensional Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization representation which is then mapped back to valid rotations $\mathbf{R}\in\text{SO}(3)$. The framework supports conditional probabilistic modeling of texture $p(\mathbf{R}|c)$, where $c$ may represent processing parameters like temperature or deformation state. To complement conventional texture-analysis visualizations, such as pole figures and sections of the orientation distribution function, we further introduce Hopf-fibration visualizations as a compact global representation of texture. TexFlow is validated on both unconditional and conditional experimental and simulated texture datasets spanning diverse material systems. We show that TexFlow can accurately capture multimodal textures and their conditional evolution, providing a data-driven framework for establishing process-texture linkages.
item.dc:creator: Gowtham Nimmal Haribabu, Tarakram Ramgopal, Divakar Vetriveeran, Siddhant Kumar

item.title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
item.description: arXiv:2610.27159v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.
item.dc:creator: Sulyman Iyanda, Mansur Arief

item.title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
item.description: arXiv:2610.27488v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.
item.dc:creator: Pei Liu

item.title: Interpretable Meta-Learning for Multi-Objective Chemical Search
item.description: arXiv:2606.20497v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Navigating the vast space of synthetically accessible molecules demands surrogate models that are interpretable and capable of handling multiple competing objectives at the same time. Deep learning approaches struggle to satisfy them under the computational constraints of quantum-level chemistry. Here, we introduce a modular pipeline that combines interpretable linear meta-learning models and adaptive-confidence uncertainty quantification into an Efficient Global Optimization (EGO) framework for multi-objective molecular discovery. For the first time, linear meta-learning is deployed in a multi-objective chemical search setting: by training across chemical objectives and cheap auxiliary properties, the meta-learned surrogates acquire transferable chemical knowledge that adapts rapidly to new objectives from limited data. Evaluated empirically on a real large scale search for spin-crossover metal-organic complexes, the baseline performs 78% worse in Pareto sense than the meta-learning alternative. We also address the calibration challenges inherent to active search. Since optimal candidates typically lie precisely in the distributional tails, standard uncertainty estimates fail. We introduce an adaptive confidence-tuning algorithm that dynamically recalibrates the exploration-exploitation trade-off as the molecular search evolves. Empirically, dynamic confidence tuning further dominates over 50% of the statically calibrated front.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Varagnolo, Yulia Pimonova, Michael G. Taylor, Rapha\"el Pestourie, Nicholas E. Lubbers

item.title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
item.description: arXiv:2606.20184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a framework that maps discrete operators onto compact, structured quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary --dense or sparse-- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems --such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry-- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki--Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator --relevant for solving partial differential equations-- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. These results motivate the extension of the framework to a broader class of operator-synthesis problems beyond the prototypical engineering and quantum applications considered here.

item.title: Recognition Is Not Grounding: Benchmarking Multilingual Financial Evidence Extraction
item.description: arXiv:2610.19432v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Comparing financial disclosures across languages requires identifying shared accounting concepts and recovering all numerical facts that express them. Existing benchmarks evaluate aspects of these capabilities, but provide limited insight into whether both succeed on the same multilingual evidence. In particular, it remains unclear whether language models can recognize these concepts across languages and exhaustively recover their corresponding numerical evidence from the same contexts. We introduce MULTIFINGROUND, a benchmark designed to investigate this recognition-grounding gap in multilingual financial reports. Constructed from FY2025 disclosures of 90 issuers in English, French, and Greek, MULTIFINGROUND aligns independently authored reports through a shared accounting taxonomy and provides traceable fact-level annotations. The benchmark evaluates financial fact identification, concept recognition, exhaustive fact selection, and concept discrimination without candidate labels. Across 15 evaluated models, eight API and open-weight reference models achieve 97.3-99.4% concept recognition accuracy, yet miss at least one target fact in 26.6-41.9% of correctly recognized groups. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in concept discrimination and limited gains from the evaluated finance-specialized models. Our findings demonstrate that strong concept recognition can coexist with incomplete evidence recovery, highlighting the importance of evaluating semantic recognition and evidence completeness together.
item.dc:creator: Lingfei Qian, Yan Wang, Xueqing Peng, Polydoros Giannouris, Nadhem Zmandar, Yi Han, Yanguang Liu, Sophia Ananiadou, V\'ictor Guti\'errez-Basulto
